content_html:
Thoughts, Neurons, and Levels of Description

Our thoughts are patterns of activity in neural networks, shaped by synaptic connections, neuromodulators, the body, and the environment, which can be described consistently across multiple intersecting levels of analysis.

Distributed Networks

It is tempting to say that our thoughts simply are neurons firing. In a strict physical sense, every conscious thought correlates with patterns of electrical activity (action potentials) in large populations of neurons and with chemical signaling at synapses. However, contemporary neuroscience shows that it is not individual spikes that matter, but structured patterns of activity in distributed networks across the brain. These are often described as population codes or distributed representations, where information is carried by the joint activity of many neurons rather than by any single cell acting in isolation.

Patterns, Timing, and Synchrony

Thoughts are better understood as population-level patterns: coordinated activity distributed across many neurons and brain regions. Work on neural population coding emphasizes how the joint activity of cells carries information, shaped by correlations and heterogeneity in the population rather than by the firing of isolated units. At the same time, the temporal structure of this activity is crucial. Oscillations and synchrony in particular frequency bands (such as gamma and related high-frequency rhythms) support flexible communication between brain regions and help bind features into coherent percepts, memories, and decisions, providing a dynamic routing mechanism for information flow in cognition and memory.

Plasticity and the Persistence of Thought

A single episode of activity is not the whole story. Over longer timescales, experience reshapes the connections between neurons through synaptic plasticity. Long-term potentiation (LTP) and related forms of plasticity in structures such as the hippocampus and cortex are widely regarded as key biological substrates of learning and memory. Repeated co-activation of cell assemblies can strengthen or weaken synaptic connections, enabling the formation, refinement, and stabilization of associative memories. In this sense, thoughts are not only momentary patterns of activity but also the history-dependent structures that make some patterns of firing easier to evoke than others in the future.

Multiple Levels of Description

Saying that “our thoughts are neurons firing” captures the implementation level, but it leaves out other levels of description that are equally real and explanatory. Following Marr's influential framework, we can distinguish at least three levels: the computational level (what problem the system is solving and why), the algorithmic/representational level (how information is represented and what procedures transform those representations), and the implementational level (how all of this is realized in physical neural tissue). A single thought can be described simultaneously as a pattern of spiking in neural circuits, as a particular computation over internal representations, and as a conscious experience with semantic content. No single level is sufficient by itself.
